newsitem.title: USA: Clinton panel on race holds first meeting.
newsitem.headline: Clinton panel on race holds first meeting.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's advisory board on race predicted on Monday its yearlong effort to shape policy would help heal the country's racial divide, and it appealed to sceptics to give it a chance.

At its first session, the seven-member panel outlined plans to open a nationwide dialogue on racism and intolerance through town hall meetings, to examine the state of race relations in America, and to provide Clinton with insight and guidance on racial issues.

"We will be the president's eyes and ears on race relations, but we also hope to be his hands and feet ... not simply a landing point, but a launching pad for action," said Suzan Johnson Cook, pastor of Bronx Christian Fellowship Church in New York.
Acknowledging the "daunting, even awesome" job ahead, former New Jersey Gov. Thomas Kean urged cynics and sceptics to "give us a chance."
"We can do no harm and, with help, we may do some good," he said.

Historian John Hope Franklin, who heads the panel, pledged to use the opportunity to make a real difference in dealing with the "virtually intractable" problem of race, which had plagued the country for more than three centuries.
Franklin, 82, of Durham, North Carolina, is a former Duke University professor to whom Clinton gave a Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1995. He wrote a landmark 1946 study, "From Slavery to Freedom."

The creation of the advisory board is part of a wider Clinton initiative to combat racism and intolerance in the United States that included a major presidential speech in California last month warning that the nation risked a return to segregation.

Clinton's recent full-scale embrace of the race issue has been received warily. Many criticise him for not taking concrete steps to address racial divisions in U.S. society, while some say his affirmative-action policies giving preference in hiring and education to members of minority groups are squeezing others out.
Clinton will go to Pittsburgh on Thursday to address the NAACP's national convention and then give a speech to the National Association of Black Journalists in Chicago.

The National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People is facing an internal debate over integration, which has been the group's goal for more than 80 years. But some in the black community now are challenging that policy, saying African Americans need to preserve their own culture.

Asked about the issue on Monday, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said: "The president believes that in this increasingly multi-ethnic, diverse society we live in that learning to live with each other is a source of our future strength, both in the world and here at home."

Clinton's advisory board has been asked to examine the state of race relations in the United States and, in a year, give Americans a report outlining "facts, not myths" about the problems and ways to solve them.

Its other members are William Winter, a former governor of Mississippi; Linda Chavez-Thompson, executive vice president of the AFL-CIO labour organisation; Robert Thomas, president and chief executive officer of Nissan USA; and Angela Oh, who helped repair race relations after the Los Angeles riots.
